text:
Panama Canal: The Panama Canal
The Panama Canal is an artificial waterway in Panama that connects the Atlantic Ocean, through the Caribbean Sea, with the Pacific Ocean. It cuts across the Isthmus of Panama and is about 82 kilometres (51 miles) long. By letting ships avoid the long voyage around the southern tip of South America, the canal became one of the most important routes in world trade.
title: Panama Canal: The Panama Canal

text:
Panama Canal: The French attempt
France made the first serious attempt to build a canal across the isthmus. The project was led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, the diplomat who had earlier developed the Suez Canal in Egypt. Work began in 1881. De Lesseps planned a sea-level canal without locks, but the mountainous terrain, heavy rainfall and landslides made this extremely difficult. Tropical diseases, especially yellow fever and malaria, killed thousands of workers. The French company went bankrupt, and the effort was abandoned in 1889.
title: Panama Canal: The French attempt

text:
Panama Canal: The American construction
The United States took over the project in 1904, shortly after Panama became independent from Colombia. The first chief engineers struggled with the same problems the French had faced. John Frank Stevens reorganised the work and supported building a canal with locks instead of a sea-level design. In 1907 he was succeeded by George Washington Goethals, an officer of the United States Army Corps of Engineers, who led the project to completion. Disease control was essential to the American success. William C. Gorgas, a United States Army physician, directed a sanitation campaign that drained standing water, controlled mosquitoes and greatly reduced yellow fever and malaria among the workforce. The most difficult section was the Culebra Cut, a deep excavation through the continental divide. It was later renamed the Gaillard Cut after David du Bose Gaillard, the engineer in charge of that section, who died before the canal opened.
title: Panama Canal: The American construction

text:
Panama Canal: How the canal works
Engineers built the Gatun Dam on the Chagres River, which created Gatun Lake. At the time it was one of the largest artificial lakes in the world. Ships are raised from sea level to the lake by sets of locks, cross the lake and the Gaillard Cut, and are then lowered back to sea level on the other side. On the original canal, the Gatun Locks serve the Atlantic side, while the Pedro Miguel Locks and the Miraflores Locks serve the Pacific side. The canal officially opened on 15 August 1914, when the cargo ship SS Ancon made the first official transit.

text:
Panama Canal: Transfer to Panama
For most of the twentieth century the United States controlled the canal and the surrounding Canal Zone. In 1977 United States President Jimmy Carter and Panamanian leader Omar Torrijos signed the Torrijos-Carter Treaties, which arranged for control of the canal to pass to Panama. The handover was completed on 31 December 1999. Since then the canal has been run by the Panama Canal Authority, an agency of the Panamanian government.
title: Panama Canal: Transfer to Panama

text:
Panama Canal: The expansion
As ships grew larger, many could no longer fit through the original locks. Panama therefore built a third set of larger locks. The expanded canal opened on 26 June 2016. The new Agua Clara Locks on the Atlantic side and the Cocoli Locks on the Pacific side can handle much larger vessels, known as Neopanamax ships. Today the Panama Canal remains a major route for global shipping and an important source of income for Panama.
